title: Sattva, rajas, tamas (14.1–14.9)
hook: three threads run through everything in nature, and through every mood you've had

segments.voice: Yesterday: seeing the same in all. One sun lights the whole world, one knower lights every field. Your line was the one light. Did you see it in a stranger? Today, what the field is woven from. Day two hundred seven.

Think about one ordinary day. At six in the morning you're heavy, foggy, you'd give anything for ten more minutes. At ten you're wired, three tabs open, answering messages while you walk. And maybe once, around sunset, there's a clear, quiet moment where everything seems simple and bright. Same person. Three completely different weathers. Hindu thought has names for those three weathers, and it says they aren't only in you. They're in food, in music, in cities, in the whole of nature. Chapter fourteen is where the Gita lays them out.
screen: `FOGGY AT SIX.` → `WIRED AT TEN.` → `CLEAR AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: Verse five. Sattva, rajas, tamas: these gunas, born of nature, bind the undying one in the body. Guna has a lovely range. It means quality, but it also means a strand, a thread, the cord of a bowstring. So picture a rope of three strands, twisted together. Everything in nature is made of all three, in different mixes. Now each one. Sattva is clarity, brightness, balance. Verse six: it's clear and it lights things up, and it's free of trouble. But even sattva binds, the Gita says, by attachment to happiness and to knowledge. You can get hooked on feeling good and feeling wise. Rajas is passion, motion, heat. Verse seven: it comes from craving and attachment, and it binds by attachment to action. It's the part of you that can't stop doing. Tamas is darkness, heaviness, inertia. Verse eight: it's born of ignorance and it deludes. It binds through carelessness, laziness and sleep. Verse nine sums it up: sattva ties you to happiness, rajas to action, tamas covers over understanding and ties you to heedlessness. Two things surprise people here. First, none of the three is simply the good one. Even the bright thread is still a thread. Second, this is a description, not a verdict. You need tamas to sleep at night and rajas to get out of bed. The point isn't to hate any strand. It's to see the rope. Our word today is the first and clearest of the three: sattva.
screen: `GUNA: A QUALITY, A THREAD.` · `SATTVA: CLEAR AND BRIGHT.` · `RAJAS: PASSION AND MOTION.` · `TAMAS: HEAVY AND DARK.` · then, large: `SATTVA.`

segments.voice: Sit, and check your own rope right now. Is there heaviness, a pull toward sleep or blankness? That's the dark thread. Is there buzzing, a list running, a wish to get up and do something? That's the moving thread. Is there any clarity, even a little, a moment of simply seeing? That's the bright one. Don't pick a favorite. Just notice the mix, the way you'd notice the weather. The bell holds the time.
Sattva. Clarity, brightness, balance: the first of the three gunas, the strands of nature, with rajas, motion, and tamas, heaviness.
Your line: three threads. Today, at three different moments, morning, midday and evening, name which thread is strongest right then. Day two hundred seven.

howItsDone: The three gunas are part of everyday Hindu vocabulary: people describe foods, habits, music and moods as sattvic, rajasic or tamasic, and Ayurveda and yoga teachers use the terms widely.

original.note: Sanskrit: guna, quality; also a strand, a thread, a bowstring. sattva, rajas and tamas are the three gunas.

trapdoor: what you thought: sattva good, rajas and tamas bad.
what it means: all three are strands of nature, all three bind, and each has its place.
what a scholar hears: the three gunas come from Samkhya thought; guna also means 'strand', and 14.5 says they bind the embodied one, sattva included (14.6).

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 14.1–14.4 (the chapter's opening: the highest knowledge; nature as the womb)

notes: 14.1–14.4 (the great Brahman as womb, Krishna as seed-giving father) is cited but not taught; a Keeper may want a line on it.
'You need tamas to sleep at night' is an interpretive teaching line, common among teachers; check tone.
